newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says it can't prove Russian ship used laser.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says it can't prove Russian ship used laser.

text.p: The United States said on Thursday an investigation had failed to confirm its suspicion that a Russian ship fired a laser at a Canadian helicopter off Washington State, injuring a U.S. Navy lieutenant.

"There is no physical evidence tying the eye injury of the American officer to a laser located on the Russian merchant vessel," the Pentagon concluded of the April 4 incident involving the fishing ship in U.S. waters off Seattle.

It said no laser had been found, but insisted again that the temporary eye injuries were "consistent with injuries that would be expected from exposure to a low-level laser, such as a laser range-finder for example."

The United States said in May that the fishing ship Kapitan Man may have illuminated the Canadian military helicopter with a laser in Puget Sound. Defence officials said the ship was suspected of spying on U.S. submarines.

Defence Secretary William Cohen told reporters at the time he was concerned over the incident, in which the Canadian helicopter pilot and the U.S. Navy lieutenant, an observer on the helicopter, received injuries.

Defence officials said privately last month that the Russian ship was suspected of spying on U.S. submarines and that the CH-124 Canadian Maritime Pacific Command helicopter was taking photographs of the ship in daylight.

The Russian government and the ship's captain denied that a laser was used, and a U.S. Coast Guard search of the Kapitan Man at Tacoma, Washington, three days after the incident found no laser device aboard.
A photograph from the helicopter showed a "bright red spot" on the ship's bridge, but that light was later determined to be a running light on the bridge of the ship.
"Specifically, the investigation could not link the officer's eye injury to a laser on the Kapitan Man or to any other location," the Pentagon said on Thursday.
Some ships carry small portable lasers as navigational aids, but there was no indication that the Kapitan Man had carried such a device.
Four Canadians and the U.S. Navy observer were aboard the helicopter at the time of the incident.
Burns to the eyes of the two men caused pain on the day after the incident, but there was apparently no permanent damage to their eyes.

The United States and other countries have conducted extensive experiments in the use of laser weapons that could disable or shoot down aircraft and even satellites, but the U.S. military has rejected the use of lasers designed to blind enemy soldiers.
